sections.h2: Where is Marion County, Oregon, and why does the layout matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Marion County sits in the Willamette Valley and covers about 1,194 square miles, with Salem as both the county seat and the largest city. It borders Yamhill, Clackamas, Wasco, Jefferson, Linn and Polk counties, so a house here can be a few minutes from the state capital or on a rural road far from it.

The county began on July 5, 1843, as the Champooick District, one of four original districts created by Oregon's Provisional Legislature. The territorial legislature renamed it for Francis Marion in 1849, and the present boundaries date to 1856. Salem became the county seat in 1849 and the state capital was confirmed there in 1864.

For a seller, the practical point is that every Marion County parcel is assessed by one office and billed by one tax collector, whether it is a Salem bungalow, a rural parcel well outside the city.

sections.h2: What drives the Marion County economy?
sections.html:
Agriculture and food processing lead the local economy, with lumber, manufacturing and education close behind. Wikipedia describes Marion County as the top agricultural producer among Oregon counties, with 10,640 acres of orchards, and the marionberry carries the county's name.

Government is the other anchor. In Salem, the State of Oregon is the largest public employer at roughly 23,500 workers, Salem Health is the largest private employer at 5,829, and Salem-Keizer School District 24J employs about 3,499. Willamette University, Corban University and Chemeketa Community College add steady local payrolls.

That mix shapes the people who end up selling a house here:

  • State and school employees who relocate for a new posting and need to close on a schedule.
  • Owners of older Salem homes who inherit a house and live out of the area.
  • Owners of rural parcels who live elsewhere and rarely see the property.

A stable government payroll tends to keep demand steady, but it does not change how the county bills tax on a house that needs work or sits vacant.

sections.h2: How do Marion County weather and wildfire affect a house you want to sell?
sections.html:
Salem has a mild, wet climate: about 40 inches of precipitation a year, most of it from October through April, with dry summers. Mean daily highs run near 48 degrees Fahrenheit in January and 83.5 in July, and snow averages about 3.5 inches a year. The all-time recorded range is minus 12 to 117 degrees.

Those numbers point to the usual wear items on an older valley house: roofs, gutters, crawl space moisture and siding that has gone through many rainy seasons. Buyers who finance often ask for repairs on those items, and sellers sometimes choose to skip that step and sell as-is.

Wildfire is a separate concern. The 2020 Santiam Fire complex burned 402,274 acres in total and destroyed nearly all of Detroit, and the fires forced large evacuations across Marion County. Owners of damaged or vacant canyon property may face questions about insurance, rebuilding and assessed value that a flat sale price does not answer. If your parcel was affected, ask the assessor how the value on your statement was set.

sections.h2: How does Marion County set the value that your tax bill is based on?
sections.html:
Marion County bills tax on assessed value, which is usually lower than real market value. Oregon's Measure 50 limits growth in assessed value on existing property to 3 percent a year, and assessed value cannot go above real market value.

Oregon's Measure 5 caps operating taxes at $10 per $1,000 of real market value for general government and $5 per $1,000 for schools. When a bill would exceed a cap, the reduction is called compression, and local option taxes are cut first. The Department of Revenue notes that Measure 50 cut taxes enough that compression has a minimal effect for most properties.

  • Real market value is the assessor's estimate of what the property would sell for.
  • Assessed value is the figure the tax rate is applied to, and new construction is valued differently from existing property.
  • Your statement lists each district that levies tax, because county, city, school and special district rates stack on one bill.

The assessor's FAQ also says most properties are not taxed on market value, which is the Measure 50 effect. A sale price well above your assessed value is therefore a separate number from the one on your statement.

sections.h2: When are Marion County property taxes due, and how do you pay?
sections.html:
Marion County mails about 124,000 tax statements between October 15 and October 25, and the main due date is November 15. If nothing has arrived by November 1, the county asks you to call the tax department.

OptionDueDiscount
Pay in fullNovember 153 percent
Pay two-thirdsNovember 15, rest by May 152 percent on the amount paid
Pay one-thirdNovember 15, then February 15 and May 15None

Payments are credited to the earliest year still owed, so a partial payment toward the current year can end up covering an old balance instead. You can pay by mail to the Marion County Tax Collection Department, by internet or phone through the county's Paystation page, or in person at Courthouse Square, 555 Court Street NE in Salem. After-hours drop boxes sit at the main entrance and in the second-floor elevator lobby.

Mailed payments need a postmark on or before the due date. Late payments lose discounts and are charged interest.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Marion County property value?
sections.html:
You can ask for an informal review by December 10 and file a formal petition with the Property Value Appeals Board by December 31. A review is not an appeal and is not required, but the Assessor's office suggests it so an appraiser can check the property and county records first.

  1. Request a review online after statements are mailed in October (real property and business personal property use separate forms).
  2. File one petition per account with the Marion County Clerk's Office. Hand delivery is accepted until 5 p.m., email and fax until midnight on December 31, and mail needs a postmark by that date.
  3. Attend a hearing of about 15 minutes. Notices go out 5 to 10 days ahead, decisions are made at the hearing, and written orders follow within 8 to 10 business days.
  4. If you disagree, file a written complaint with the Oregon Tax Court Magistrate Division within 30 days after the order is mailed.
  5. A magistrate's decision can be taken to the Regular Division within 60 days.

Evidence should show market value as of January 1 of the assessment year. Hearings are held at Courthouse Square, 555 Court Street NE, second floor, and can be arranged by video or phone in advance. The Clerk's phone is (503) 588-3578 and the Assessor's is (503) 588-5144.

sections.h2: What happens if property taxes go unpaid in Marion County?
sections.html:
Marion County must start foreclosure on a property once its oldest unpaid tax year is three years delinquent. Real property tax becomes delinquent on May 16, so taxes unpaid from 2022-23 became subject to foreclosure on May 16, 2026.

  • June: delinquent notices go out, stating when foreclosure would begin.
  • July and August: letters go to owners, and payments must be cash or cashier's check from that point.
  • August 16 or later: the list is published and the county applies for judgment in circuit court. A 5 percent penalty is added to the tax and interest.
  • About 30 days after publication: judgment is granted and a two-year redemption period starts.
  • Two years after judgment: redemption ends and the property is deeded to the county.

During redemption only parties with a recorded interest as of the judgment date can pay, and partial payments are not accepted. The tax office can be reached at 503-588-5215 or propertytax@co.marion.or.us. Owners who are behind and cannot catch up often look at a quick sale before the publication date, since that is when the cost jumps.

sections.h2: What should a Marion County seller do about taxes before closing?
sections.html:
Ask the tax office for the current balance and any delinquent years before you sign, because older years are paid first. The county pages we read do not describe how tax is split between buyer and seller at closing, so that part is handled by the escrow or title company that prepares the settlement statement.

A short checklist keeps surprises away:

  • Pull your latest statement and confirm the account number and mailing address.
  • Check whether a mortgage servicer has been paying through an impound account.
  • Make sure the county has a mailing address that will still work after the sale.
  • Tell the title company about unpaid years so the payoff figure is right.

Deeds are recorded through the County Clerk's records office, which keeps its own fee schedule and first-page rules. Documents that miss the first-page requirements can draw a cover sheet fee.

This page is general information and not tax advice. Confirm dates with the county before you rely on them.

faqs.q: When is the Marion County property tax due date?
faqs.a: The main due date is November 15. Pay in full by then for a 3 percent discount, pay two-thirds for 2 percent with the rest due May 15, or pay one-third with later installments on February 15 and May 15 and no discount.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Marion County property value?
faqs.a: File with the Marion County Clerk's Office no later than December 31. An informal review request is due by December 10 and is optional. If December 31 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

faqs.q: Where do I send a Marion County property tax payment?
faqs.a: Mail to the Marion County Tax Collection Dept., PO Box 3416, Portland, OR 97208-3416, postmarked by the due date, or pay through the county's Paystation page. In person payments go to Courthouse Square, 555 Court Street NE, Salem.

faqs.q: How long before Marion County can foreclose for unpaid tax?
faqs.a: Foreclosure starts when the oldest unpaid year is three years delinquent. After judgment there is a two-year redemption period, and the property is deeded to the county if it is not redeemed.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Marion County house if I owe back taxes?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the back taxes are paid from the sale at closing. Payments go to the oldest year first, so ask the tax office for a payoff figure and give it to the escrow or title company.
